radon.actionLevel: EPA recommends fixing a home if the radon level is 4 pCi/L or more; EPA gives the equivalent as 150 Bq/m3 (exact conversion is 148 Bq/m3 because 1 pCi/L = 37 Bq/m3; EPA rounds). EPA says there is no known safe level of radon exposure. Average indoor level is about 1.3 pCi/L (50 Bq/m3) and outdoor air about 0.4 pCi/L (15 Bq/m3). EPA's best estimate is about 21,000 radon-related lung cancer deaths a year.
radon.considerFixing: EPA says to consider fixing a home with levels between 2 and 4 pCi/L (75-150 Bq/m3). Levels below 4 pCi/L still carry some risk, and EPA says most homes today can be reduced to 2 pCi/L or below.
radon.testTypes: Short-term tests stay in the home 2 to 90 days (charcoal canisters, alpha track, electret ion chamber, continuous monitors, charcoal liquid scintillation); long-term tests stay more than 90 days (alpha track, electret) and better reflect the year-round average. EPA's steps: (1) take a short-term test; (2) if the result is 4 pCi/L or higher, follow up with a long-term test (better year-round picture) or a second short-term test (faster; do it immediately if the first result is more than twice 4 pCi/L); (3) fix the home if the long-term result is 4 pCi/L or more, or consider fixing if the average of the two short-term tests is 4 pCi/L or more. Place the test in the lowest lived-in level, in a regularly used room (not a kitchen or bathroom), at least 20 inches above the floor, away from drafts, heat, humidity and exterior walls; keep windows and doors closed (for 2-3 day tests, starting at least 12 hours before), and don't run 2-3 day tests during severe storms or high winds. For home sales, EPA's Home Buyer's and Seller's Guide (revised March 2024) accepts three short-term options: two passive tests side by side for at least 48 hours, two back-to-back passive tests of at least 48 hours each, or a continuous monitor for at least 48 hours; fix if the average is 4 pCi/L or more, and take steps to prevent or detect device interference.
radon.zones: EPA's Map of Radon Zones (developed in 1993) assigns each county a zone by predicted average indoor radon: Zone 1 (red) highest potential, average indoor levels may be greater than 4 pCi/L; Zone 2 (orange) moderate, 2-4 pCi/L; Zone 3 (yellow) low, less than 2 pCi/L. It exists to help national, state and local organizations target resources and adopt radon-resistant building codes. EPA says it must not be used to decide whether to test a home: high levels turn up in all three zones and every home should be tested. Map page: https://www.epa.gov/radon/epa-map-radon-zones ; PDF map: https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-05/radon-zones-map_text_link.pdf ; county list (XLS): https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-05/radon_zones-spreadsheet.xls . EPA's page does not link an interactive map.
radon.certification: EPA requires states that receive indoor radon grants to keep a public list of credentialed providers, credentialed either through a state process (such as a state license) or through one of two national proficiency programs. NRPP (National Radon Proficiency Program, accredited by ANAB to ISO/IEC 17024; renewal every two years): find a pro at https://nrpp.info/pro-search/ (search by certification type, last name or NRPP ID). NRSB (National Radon Safety Board): find a pro at https://nrsb.org/find-a-pro/ (search by state, ZIP and radius, name, certification type or company). Where a state licenses radon work, the state list governs who may legally work there. EPA's locator page: https://www.epa.gov/radon/find-radon-test-kit-or-measurement-and-mitigation-professional ; discounted test kits are sold by National Radon Program Services at Kansas State University (https://sosradon.org/test-kits), and some states give free or discounted kits.

stateLicensing.requirement: No one may provide radon measurement or mitigation services to the public unless they hold NRPP or NRSB certification and are on CDPH's certified list (Health & Safety Code 106750-106795; certificate copy submitted to CDPH, renewed every 2 years, no state fee). Mitigators must also hold a CSLB contractor license (B, C20, C36 or D64).

State license (Division of Professions and Occupations, DORA) required for radon measurement and mitigation professionals since July 1, 2022 (C.R.S. 12-165-101 to -113); per AARST, private certification is required to qualify for and keep the license; work must follow ANSI/AARST standards. Exempt: people testing or mitigating a single-family home they own and occupy, or a unit they lease/occupy.

Radon mitigators must hold NRPP or NRSB certification and a Home Improvement Contractor registration from the Dept. of Consumer Protection (C.G.S. 20-419 to -420). No state credential for radon testers was found.

Anyone conducting radon screening, testing or mitigation for a fee must be listed as proficient by EPA or certified by a Mayor-approved organization (D.C. Code 28-4201); DOEE rules (20 DCMR 3250) require NRPP or NRSB certification.

State certification by the Florida Dept. of Health for radon measurement and mitigation businesses and individuals (technicians, specialists); all mitigation must be done by state-certified professionals (F.S. 404.056; F.A.C. 64E-5 Part XII).

IEMA-OHS license required to perform radon measurement or mitigation (professional and technician licenses; Radon Industry Licensing Act, 420 ILCS 44; 32 Ill. Adm. Code 422). Active mitigation systems in new homes must be installed by licensed radon contractors (Radon Resistant Construction Act, 420 ILCS 52).
Anyone doing radon testing, analysis or mitigation in homes must be certified by the Indiana Department of Health (410 IAC 5.1); tester categories: laboratory, primary, secondary; plus mitigator.
Iowa HHS certifies radon measurement specialists and laboratories and credentials radon mitigation specialists (Iowa Code 136B; 641 IAC chapters 43 and 44).

All persons performing radon testing or mitigation must be certified by KDHE (Kansas Radon Certification Act, passed 2010, effective 2011): measurement technicians, mitigation technicians and measurement laboratories.

Radon measurement, mitigation and laboratory businesses/contractors must hold NRPP or NRSB certification (since June 2019) and register with the Kentucky Board of Radon Safety (KRS 309.430-.454; Board created July 2022).
Radon testers and mitigators must register with Maine DHHS (Radon Registration Act, 22 M.R.S. 771-784; 10-144 CMR ch. 224).

MDH license required for measurement professionals, mitigation professionals, mitigation companies and radon analysis labs (Minnesota Radon Licensing Act, Minn. Stat. 144.4961, signed May 2015); installed systems get an MDH mitigation system tag.
Anyone working in a radon occupation must be licensed by DHHS (measurement and mitigation specialists), as must measurement and mitigation businesses (180 NAC 11; Radiation Control Act).

Anyone designing or installing airborne radon mitigation systems must hold current NRPP or NRSB certification (RSA 310-A:189-a, effective Jan 1, 2015). No state credential for radon testers was found.

All radon testing and mitigation businesses and individuals must be certified by NJDEP; only certified individuals or the homeowner may test or mitigate a home (N.J.S.A. 26:2D-70 to -80; N.J.A.C. 7:28-27). Labs are certified under N.J.A.C. 7:18.
Ohio Department of Health licenses radon testers, mitigation specialists and mitigation contractors (ORC 3723.02); per ELI, laboratories are also licensed (ORC 3723; OAC 3701-69).
DEP certification required to place/retrieve radon test devices, to mitigate, and to analyze radon devices received from the public (25 Pa. Code ch. 240).
State certification or licensure of radon measurement and mitigation professionals and radon analytical services by RIDOH (R.I. Gen. Laws 23-61; 216-RICR-50-15-2).

Installation, repair or replacement of a radon mitigation system must be done by a licensed Utah contractor (SB 163, effective May 12, 2009; Utah Code 58-55-305); DEQ advises also checking for NRPP certification. No testing credential. HB 563 (2026), which would have added radon mitigation training/certification, failed (per a third-party bill tracker).
Radon testers and mitigators must hold current NRSB or NRPP certification to legally test or mitigate (Va. Code 32.1-229.01); per ELI, contractor licensing also has a radon mitigation specialty.

State licenses required for radon testers, mitigation specialists, mitigation contractors and radon laboratories (W. Va. Code 16-34-3). HB 5625 (2026), a Department of Health bill amending the licensing article, was reported from committee Feb 24, 2026; final status not verified.

radon.realEstate: EPA's sales guidance points buyers to state or local disclosure rules, and no federal radon disclosure rule (like the federal lead rule) appeared in the EPA materials reviewed. EPA's sales guidance says to test before listing, test the lowest level a buyer might use, and expect buyers to ask for a new test if the last one is more than about two years old or the home has been renovated. EPA notes a buyer may also ask for a new test 'if your state or local government requires disclosure of radon information to buyers'. AARST counted ten states with homebuyer radon awareness-notification laws as of June 2024: CO, DE, FL, IL, IA, KS, MN, MT, NH and RI. Notable rules: Illinois Radon Awareness Act (420 ILCS 46) requires sellers to give buyers the IEMA pamphlet 'Radon Testing Guidelines for Real Estate Transactions' and a signed 'Disclosure of Information on Radon Hazards' before the buyer is obligated; no testing is required and units on the third floor or higher are exempt. Minnesota Radon Awareness Act: before a purchase agreement, sellers disclose known tests, the most current records, any mitigation system details, a radon warning statement and MDH's 'Radon in Real Estate Transactions'; testing is not required. Colorado SB 23-206 (C.R.S. 38-35.7-112 and 38-12-803): sales contracts must carry a bold radon warning, sellers disclose known test results and mitigation and give the CDPHE radon brochure, and landlords must make similar pre-lease disclosures. Tenants may void a lease if the landlord fails to disclose, or fails to make a reasonable effort to mitigate within 180 days of a 4 pCi/L-or-higher reading; from Jan 1, 2026 this voiding right does not apply to leases of one year or less. Florida requires a radon notification statement on at least one sale or rental document (F.S. 404.056). New Jersey sellers must give buyers copies of any radon test results on entering a contract (N.J.S.A. 26:2D-70 et seq., per ELI). Maine required radon testing of residential rentals by 2012, with written notice of results to tenants and mitigation within six months when results are 4 pCi/L or higher. North Dakota now requires written seller disclosure of known radon information, test results and mitigation (NDCC 47-10-02.2; newly listed in ELI's June 2026 database). Missouri DHSS says radon professionals must be used for testing tied to legal transactions. Changed in 2026: Iowa HF 2297 (approved May 19, 2026) requires passive radon mitigation in new one- and two-family homes once the building code commissioner adopts the rule.
radon.mitigationCost: EPA (page updated Sep 16, 2026) gives no dollar figure: 'Most homes can be fixed for about the same cost as other common home repairs', with costs depending on the home's size and design and the method needed; get estimates from several qualified mitigators. A passive system installed during construction costs much less to activate later. National Radon Program Services (Kansas State University, EPA-funded) puts typical contractor pricing at $800 to about $2,500, averaging about $1,200; this is an older figure. Minnesota's health department warns against unlicensed installers and unusually low bids (under $1,000).
radon.notes: The state licensing list combines ELI's state radon law database (laws enacted through June 2026) with each state's own program page or statute. Not counted as licensing: Maryland Environment 8-305, which requires radon testing businesses to have tests analyzed by facilities listed in EPA's National Radon Measurement Proficiency Program and to give written results, but sets up no state license; Montana, where radon professionals must pass an EPA proficiency exam only to be publicly listed; North Carolina, which voluntarily approves certifying bodies (final rule 10A NCAC 15.1801 took effect May 2025) and does not require individual certification; and Delaware, which says it does not certify radon contractors (2019 list). State agencies confirm no radon licensing in Texas, Michigan and Massachusetts. New York does not license mitigators, and no tester licensing was found. Georgia has no certification law for mitigators. Missouri HB 2730 (2026), which would have licensed radon professionals from 2027, was referred to committee on May 15, 2026 and did not pass. After the WebSearch budget ran out, state law changes after June 2026 were checked only where noted (MO, UT, WV, IA).

carbonMonoxide.alarmStandard: UL 2034, Standard for Single and Multiple Station Carbon Monoxide Alarms. Edition 5 is current: published June 3, 2024 and last revised Aug 7, 2024, so it changed in 2024. It covers electrically operated single- and multiple-station CO alarms for indoor spaces and unconditioned areas, including RVs, mobile homes and boats. Alarms must sound below CO levels that impair a person's ability to react, and must resist false alarms from long-term low-level or brief transient CO (for example, air pollution or properly working appliances). CPSC points consumers to the current UL 2034 standard. Several state laws require alarms listed to ANSI/UL 2034 or ANSI/UL 2075 (for example, N.C. G.S. 42-42 and Michigan MCL 125.1504f).
carbonMonoxide.guidance: CPSC recommends CO alarms on every level of the home and outside sleeping areas, ideally interconnected so that when one sounds, all sound. Keep alarms away from heating vents and anywhere furniture or drapes could block them; CPSC does not recommend placing them in kitchens or above fuel-burning appliances. Battery-operated alarms, or plug-in or hard-wired alarms with battery backup, are recommended. The test button checks the circuitry, not sensor accuracy. Replace alarms at the replacement age in the product literature; CPSC gives no fixed number of years. For audits, BPI-1200 sets ambient CO action levels: 9-35 ppm, advise checking sources and ventilating; 36-69 ppm, ventilate and turn off sources; 70 ppm or more, stop work and evacuate.

stateLaws.requirement: Executive Law 378(5-a): every one- or two-family dwelling, condo or co-op dwelling unit, and multiple dwelling must have an operable CO detector where the unit has CO-emitting appliances, devices or systems, or an attached garage. The statute sets no construction-date cutoff.

N.J.S.A. 52:27D-133.3 to -133.5: CO detectors in one- and two-family homes at initial occupancy or change of occupancy (sale or new tenancy); separate statutes cover hotels, multiple dwellings and rooming houses unless no CO hazard exists. Fire Code rules (N.J.A.C. 5:70-4.9(d), 4.19) require CO detection in existing buildings with a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage.

Act 121 of 2013 (Carbon Monoxide Alarm Standards Act, effective Dec 18, 2013): on sale of a residential building the seller must disclose CO detector information on the property disclosure statement. Each apartment in a multifamily dwelling with a fossil-fuel heater or appliance, fireplace or attached garage must have an approved, centrally located CO alarm near the bedrooms (owner installs; tenant maintains). Municipalities may adopt stricter rules.

Health & Safety Code 17926: owners must install a State Fire Marshal-listed CO device in each existing dwelling unit with a fossil-fuel heater or appliance, fireplace or attached garage, by July 1, 2011 for single-family homes, Jan 1, 2013 for other dwellings and Jan 1, 2017 for hotels and motels. Sellers disclose CO devices on the transfer disclosure form (Civ. Code 1102, per ELI).

Carbon Monoxide Alarm Detector Act (430 ILCS 135/10): every dwelling unit must have at least one approved, operating CO alarm within 15 feet of every room used for sleeping; multi-unit structures also need at least one.

No statewide residential CO-alarm statute found. NCSL lists only Hum. Res. Code 42.060, which requires CO detectors in qualifying day-care centers, group day-care homes and family homes. Municipalities apply the IRC as it existed May 1, 2012 as their residential code (Loc. Gov't Code 214.212); its CO-alarm section was not verified here.

Georgia State Minimum Standard One and Two Family Dwelling Code (R313.4.1, R315.2.1, adopted under O.C.G.A. 8-2-20): CO detectors in general sleeping areas of all new one- and two-family homes and townhomes of three stories or less. New construction only.

F.S. 553.885: every building or addition built on or after July 1, 2008 with a fossil-fuel heater or appliance, fireplace, attached garage or other CO source needs an approved CO alarm within 10 feet of each room used for sleeping (hard-wired or battery, or combination smoke/CO). Does not apply to existing homes unless an addition is built.
D.C. Code 6-751.02: the owner of every new and existing occupied dwelling unit must install smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors in accordance with the DC Construction Codes.

Per NCSL: Va. Code 27-94 et seq. and 36-97 et seq. set a statewide standard for installing and maintaining smoke and CO alarms in rental properties under the Statewide Fire Prevention Code. The landlord's annual certification (Va. Code 55.1-1220) covers smoke alarms. The fire-code CO provisions were not opened.

Public Safety 12-1101 to -1106: applies to new dwellings using fossil fuel with building permits issued on or after Jan 1, 2008, and to hotels, rooming houses and rental dwelling units. A CO alarm goes in a central location outside each sleeping area; rental units since April 1, 2018 need alarms outside each sleeping area and on each level including the basement; hotels since April 1, 2017. Per NCSL, sellers of single-family homes must disclose fossil-fuel heating and alarm installation.

M.G.L. c.148 s.26F1/2: every residential building with fossil-fuel equipment (furnace, boiler, water heater, fireplace) or enclosed parking must have working, approved CO alarms. Landlords install them and must have them working at the start of each rental. The fire department inspects for compliance on sale or transfer.

stateLaws.notes: No Arizona statute appears in NCSL's compilation (updated Sep 29, 2025), and none was found elsewhere. Local codes may require CO alarms in new construction. Absence not independently confirmed.

stateLaws.requirement: MCL 125.1504f (effective Mar 23, 2009): the state construction code may require at least one CO device in new single- and multifamily dwellings, renovations needing a permit, and bedroom additions. Devices go near bedrooms, next to an attached garage and next to fuel-burning appliances, and must be listed to ANSI/UL 2034 or UL 2075. The requirement applies through the adopted residential code; it is not a retrofit mandate for existing homes.

RCW 19.27.530: CO alarms required in newly built residential occupancies (code by Jan 1, 2011) and all other residential buildings by Jan 1, 2013. Owner-occupied single-family homes legally occupied before July 26, 2009 are exempt, but when one is sold the seller must install CO alarms before the buyer occupies it.

Minn. Stat. 299F.51: every single-family dwelling and every multifamily dwelling unit must have an approved, working CO alarm within 10 feet of each room lawfully used for sleeping. Multifamily owners install and replace alarms between tenancies; occupants maintain them; disabling an alarm is prohibited.

C.R.S. 38-45-101 to -106 (per NCSL): existing single-family homes and multifamily units offered for sale or transfer (on or after a specified date) that have a fuel-burning heater or appliance, fireplace or attached garage must have an operational CO alarm within a specified distance of each sleeping room; a similar rule applies to new residential construction. The statute text was not opened; leg.colorado.gov blocked automated access.

stateLaws.notes: No Missouri statute appears in NCSL's compilation (updated Sep 29, 2025), and none was found elsewhere. Local ordinances or adopted building codes may apply. Absence not independently confirmed.

stateLaws.requirement: G.S. 42-42(a)(7): landlords must provide at least one operable CO alarm per rental unit per level in units with a fossil-fuel heater, appliance or fireplace, or an attached garage. Alarms must be listed to ANSI/UL 2034 or 2075, working at the start of each tenancy, and repaired or replaced within 15 days of written notice. Per NCSL, G.S. 143-138 also authorizes State Building Code rules requiring CO detectors in dwelling units with fossil-fuel sources or attached garages.

ORS 105.836-.842: one- and two-family dwellings and multifamily housing with a CO source (fuel-burning heater, fireplace, appliance or cooking source, or an attached garage) can't be sold or transferred unless working CO alarms cover all sleeping areas; buyers may sue for the greater of actual damages or $250 per unit. ORS 90.317: landlords must provide CO alarms in such units and give written testing instructions; CO alarms are a habitability requirement.

lead.pre1978: EPA: a home built before 1978 is more likely to have lead-based paint; the federal government banned consumer uses of lead-based paint in 1978, and some states banned it earlier. EPA says the most common source of lead exposure is dust from lead-based paint in older homes. Lead is especially dangerous to children 6 and younger. CDC's blood lead reference value is 3.5 ug/dL, and EPA notes CDC recommends testing children at 12 and 24 months.
lead.rrpRule: Anyone paid to do work that disturbs paint in housing or child-occupied facilities (child care centers, preschools) built before 1978 must be lead-safe certified by EPA or an authorized state, sole proprietors included. Firms must use certified renovators trained by EPA-accredited providers and follow lead-safe work practices. Covered work includes remodeling, repair and maintenance, electrical, plumbing, painting prep, carpentry and window replacement. Exempt: minor repair and maintenance disturbing 6 sq ft of paint or less per room inside, or 20 sq ft or less outside; window replacement and demolition of painted surfaces are always covered. Also excluded: housing for the elderly or disabled and zero-bedroom units (unless a child under 6 lives there), and components certified lead-free. Firms must give occupants EPA's 'Lead-Safe Certified Guide to Renovate Right' no more than 60 days before work starts. EPA tells homeowners in pre-1978 homes to hire a lead-safe certified contractor and check the firm in EPA's locator. Fifteen states run their own RRP programs instead of EPA: AL, DE, GA, IA, KS, MA, MS, NC, OK, OR, RI, UT, VT, WA and WI (plus the Bois Forte Band); a contractor working in several states may need both EPA and state certification.
lead.disclosure: Under the federal lead disclosure rule (Section 1018 of the Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act of 1992), sellers and landlords of housing built before 1978 must: disclose any known lead-based paint and lead hazards; hand over available records and reports; give buyers or renters EPA's pamphlet 'Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home'; and put a Lead Warning Statement in or attached to the contract or lease. Buyers get 10 days to arrange a lead-based paint inspection or risk assessment; the parties can change the period in writing, or the buyer can waive it. Landlords don't have to provide an inspection. Signed disclosures must be kept for 3 years. Exempt: zero-bedroom units and elderly or disabled housing (unless a child under 6 lives there), leases of 100 days or less, housing certified lead-free, foreclosure sales, and housing built after 1977.
lead.inspectionVsRiskAssessment: EPA: a lead-based paint inspection tells you whether a building has lead-based paint and where it is, but not whether hazards exist now. A risk assessment tells you whether there are lead hazards from paint, dust or soil, and what to do about them. Both must be done by EPA- or state-certified inspectors or risk assessors working for certified firms. EPA runs the abatement, inspection and risk-assessment program directly in AK, AZ, FL, ID, MT, NV, NM, NY, SC, SD and WY (plus territories and most tribal lands); every other state has an EPA-authorized program.
lead.dustStandards2024: Changed in 2024. EPA finalized the rule in October 2024 (Federal Register Nov 12, 2024); it took effect January 13, 2025. The dust-lead hazard standard, renamed the 'dust-lead reportable level', dropped from 10 ug/ft2 (floors) and 100 ug/ft2 (window sills) to any reportable level as analyzed by an EPA-recognized (NLLAP) lab. Post-abatement clearance, renamed 'dust-lead action levels', dropped to 5 ug/ft2 for floors (from 10), 40 ug/ft2 for sills (from 100) and 100 ug/ft2 for window troughs (from 400). The rule decouples the hazard and clearance standards and redefines abatement so EPA recommends it at or above the action levels; between the reportable and action levels, EPA recommends HEPA vacuuming and wet cleaning instead. The 2024 levels replace those set in 2001, 2019 and 2021. Separate compliance deadlines (for example, for authorized state programs) could not be confirmed from the text opened; EPA's page (updated Dec 19, 2025) lists no later changes. The rule says EPA plans to propose soil-lead hazard standards in 2026.
lead.drinkingWater: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, finalized Oct 8, 2024 (Federal Register Oct 30, 2024). Most water systems must identify and replace lead and galvanized-requiring-replacement service lines under their control within 10 years; limited deferrals are allowed. The lead action level drops from 0.015 to 0.010 mg/L (15 to 10 ug/L), the separate trigger level is removed, and tap sampling becomes stricter. By Nov 1, 2027 systems must submit their baseline service line inventory and a replacement plan, and from that date the new action level triggers Tier 1 public notice. Systems with repeated exceedances must offer certified lead-reducing filters. Status Oct 2026: EPA's LCRI pages (updated Dec 29, 2025) and supporting-materials page (live HTML dated Oct 5, 2026) still show the 2024 rule and dates with no announced extension. Other 2025-2026 EPA announcements, litigation or proposals could not be checked once the search budget ran out.

asbestos.homeowners: EPA: leave asbestos material that is in good condition and won't be disturbed alone. If it is damaged, or remodeling will disturb it, have a trained and accredited asbestos professional assess it; repair or removal must be done only by trained and accredited professionals. Don't take samples yourself: a professional should do it, because sampling can release fibers. Use different firms for inspection and for repair or removal to avoid a conflict of interest. Federal law does not require accreditation for most work in detached single-family homes, but some states and localities do, so check state and local rules before any work.
asbestos.vermiculite: EPA: the mine near Libby, Montana supplied more than 70 percent of all vermiculite sold in the U.S. from 1919 to 1990, and it was contaminated with asbestos. If you have vermiculite attic or wall insulation, assume it may contain asbestos. Leave it undisturbed, limit trips into the attic, and do not try to remove it yourself; for renovation that would disturb it, hire a professional asbestos contractor. EPA warns that testing an attic can be expensive and, depending on the method, may give erroneous results, and it does not recommend opening walls to look for vermiculite.
asbestos.inspectors: EPA's Asbestos Model Accreditation Plan (MAP) requires training for five disciplines: worker, contractor/supervisor, inspector, management planner and project designer. States must meet at least the MAP minimums; some states accredit people directly and others approve training providers, so the state agency is the source for who may work there (EPA keeps a state asbestos contacts directory). Asbestos labs are accredited through NIST's NVLAP. School (AHERA) samples must go to an NVLAP lab, and EPA recommends NVLAP or equivalent for other samples.

mold.federal: EPA does not regulate mold or mold spores in indoor air, and there are no EPA or other federal limits for mold or spores, so sampling can't show compliance with any federal standard. EPA says sampling is usually unnecessary when mold is visible; surface sampling may help confirm an area was cleaned, and should be done by experienced professionals. Fix the water problem, dry everything, scrub hard surfaces with detergent and water, and discard porous materials such as ceiling tiles or carpet that stay moldy. Don't paint or caulk over mold. If the moldy area is less than about 10 sq ft (roughly 3 ft by 3 ft), you can usually handle it yourself; for larger areas or significant water damage, follow EPA's 'Mold Remediation in Schools and Commercial Buildings'.

stateLicensing.requirement: State license from TDLR required for mold assessment and mold remediation (Occupations Code ch. 1958; 16 TAC ch. 78). One licensee may not do both assessment and remediation on the same project (school-district employees excepted). Exemptions include visible mold under 25 contiguous sq ft and some owner/building exemptions (for example, residential buildings with fewer than 10 units). Assessors must give clients a Consumer Mold Information Sheet.
DBPR licenses mold assessors and mold remediators (F.S. 468.84-.8424; F.A.C. 61-31). Licenses expire July 31 of even years (latest deadline July 31, 2026).

NY DOL license required to work, advertise or hold out as a mold assessor or mold remediation contractor; abatement workers are also licensed (Labor Law Article 32, sections 930-948). The same person may not do both assessment and remediation on one property; owners working on their own residential property are exempt.

LSLBC Mold Remediation license required for remediation projects worth $7,500 or more; the qualifying party needs 24 hours of training in mold remediation and basic mold assessment (La. R.S. 37:2150.1, 2156-2158). The same contractor may not do both assessment and remediation on one property.

DOEE licenses individual mold assessors and remediators (exam, 2-year license, $1M insurance; D.C. Code 8-241.01-.09; 20 DCMR ch. 32). In rentals, landlords must use DOEE-licensed assessors and remediators for mold areas of 10 sq ft or more; smaller areas may be cleaned by unlicensed workers.

Paid residential mold assessment requires a valid national third-party mold assessment certification (RSA 310-A:189-b). Not a state license; professionals whose main contracted work is not mold assessment are exempt.

It is a prohibited practice under the Consumer Protection Act to sell professional mold remediation for a home without a mold remediation certification from a nationally or internationally recognized body, or to skip EPA's Mold Remediation in Schools and Commercial Buildings, ANSI/IICRC S520 or an equivalent standard (Va. Code 59.1-200(A)(81)). Not a state license. 2025 HB 2195 had DPOR study whether to license mold inspectors and remediators (report due Jan 1, 2026); outcome not verified.
Not mold-specific: residential mold remediation over $200 counts as 'home improvement', so the contractor needs a Home Improvement Contractor registration from DCP (C.G.S. 20-419 to -420), per ELI.
Not mold-specific: mold remediation falls under the contractor board's Specialty/Environmental license classification (Tenn. Code 62-6-112; Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 0680-01-.16), per ELI.

wellWater.federal: EPA: private domestic wells are not regulated by the federal Safe Drinking Water Act, nor by most states; owners are responsible for making sure their water is safe. About 15 percent of Americans (more than 43 million people, over 23 million households) use private wells. In a USGS study of 2,100 domestic wells, about one in five had at least one contaminant above a human-health benchmark, mostly naturally occurring metals, radionuclides and nitrate; bacteria were found in about a third of the roughly 400 wells tested for microbes.
wellWater.testAnnually: EPA: test a private well every year for total coliform bacteria, nitrates, total dissolved solids and pH. Test more often if young children, older adults, or someone pregnant or nursing lives there. Test right away after flooding, land disturbance or nearby construction or industrial activity; after repairing or replacing any part of the well system; if taste, odor or color changes; or if there are known groundwater problems in the area. Ask the local health department what is common in local groundwater.
wellWater.otherContaminants: EPA's triggers: recurring stomach illness, test for coliform; lead plumbing or corrosion, test pH, lead and copper; radon in indoor air or a radon-rich area, test for radon; intensive farming nearby, test nitrate, nitrite, pesticides and coliform; mining nearby, test metals and pH; gas drilling nearby, test chloride, sodium, barium and strontium; landfills, gas stations or dry cleaners nearby, or a fuel odor, test VOCs. EPA lists arsenic among heavy metals and uranium among radionuclides that can occur in wells (radionuclides can harm kidneys and raise cancer risk). USGS estimates about 2.1 million people use wells high in arsenic (over 10 ug/L, the public-water MCL); about 7 percent of drinking-water aquifer wells sampled nationally exceeded it, about 16 percent in the Southwest, and arsenic is more common in the West, the glacial aquifer system and several eastern and southern aquifers. PFAS: private wells fall outside the Safe Drinking Water Act, so EPA's PFAS limits don't apply to them; for reference, the 2024 public-water limits are PFOA and PFOS 4.0 ppt and PFHxS, PFNA and GenX 10 ppt, plus a mixture hazard index. EPA's 2024 funding announcement included help for private well owners dealing with PFAS. Changed in 2025-2026: EPA said on May 14, 2025 it would keep the PFOA and PFOS limits, and on May 18, 2026 proposed two rules for public comment: one lets systems request two more years (to 2031) to comply, and one would rescind the limits for PFHxS, PFNA, GenX and the hazard index. Whether either has been finalized since May 18, 2026 was not verified.
wellWater.certifiedLabs: Use only labs certified for drinking-water testing. EPA links each state's lab certification program in a PDF: https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2023-03/state-cert-programs-certify-labs-to-conduct-drinking-water-analyses.pdf (from https://www.epa.gov/dwlabcert/contact-information-certification-programs-and-certified-laboratories-drinking-water). Local health departments may test private wells for free. EPA does not test home water on request.

combustionSafety.standard: ANSI/BPI-1200-S-2017, Standard Practice for Basic Analysis of Buildings, is still listed on BPI's standards page. Its Section 7 adopts the combustion-appliance inspection requirements of BPI-1100 Section 7 and adds to them; the current BPI-1100 is ANSI/BPI-1100-T-2023 (Home Energy Auditing Standard). Before testing, the auditor checks combustible gas (below 10% of the lower explosive limit) and ambient CO (below 70 ppm). Ambient CO action levels: 9-35 ppm, advise; 36-69 ppm, ventilate and shut off sources; 70 ppm or more, stop, evacuate and call emergency services from outside. The combustion appliance safety test sets up the greatest depressurization achievable in the combustion appliance zone (CAZ) for the conditions, then measures spillage and CO on natural-draft appliances (barometric draft control) and Category I appliances (draft hood or natural-draft vent), plus CO on gas ovens and direct-vent or vent-free equipment. DOE's Building America Solution Center calls for CAZ testing in homes with natural-draft furnaces, boilers or water heaters, especially when air sealing (at the end of each workday). It cites NFPA 54 for combustion air, and RESNET Section 805 / ANSI/ACCA 12 QH-2014 Appendix A (CO test and CAZ depressurization test) for ENERGY STAR homes keeping non-direct-vent appliances in climate zones 1-3.

hersIndex.summary: RESNET's HERS Index is the industry standard home energy rating. A certified RESNET HERS Rater rates the home against a computer-modeled reference home of the same size and shape. A home built to 2006 energy standards (the 2006 IECC) scores 100, and lower is better: 70 means 30% more efficient than the reference home, 130 means 30% less efficient, and 0 means net zero energy. Ratings are calculated under ANSI/RESNET/ICC 301 and tested under 380. HERS uses 301-2019 through Dec 31, 2026, and 301-2022 (with 380-2022) is mandatory from Jan 1, 2027; 301-2025 will be allowed voluntarily once software is updated. RESNET's public registry verifies raters and shows ratings for rated homes. Find a rater: https://www.hersindex.com/find-a-hers-rater/
